title: smallest-board demo, service and infrastructure
description:
Two small public repos under tanya-ok that consume the ecs-contract end to end, so the pattern reads as working code and not only a specification.

Subject: 3x3 Go. The smallest board on which Go is still Go. All rules intact in nine points (liberties, capture, no suicide, ko, positional superko, area scoring), and the game is solved: 12675 legal positions; under Tromp rules with positional superko Black wins 9-0 opening in the centre, and by 3 opening on the edge (source: Hayward, University of Alberta, solving Go on small boards; Tromp, counting legal positions). Rules of a board game are not copyrightable and both sources are public, so the demo is legally clean.

Framing for the README: the two-writer problem is a ko fight, two systems recapturing the same position in turn. Positional superko forbids returning to any previous whole-board position; the ownership contract does the same for the task definition, and the drift audit compares whole positions rather than single stones. Second layer: the game is completely solved and still worth playing.

Repo smallest-board (service): a small HTTP service in Python, full 3x3 rules, an oracle endpoint returning perfect play, game records in Postgres. Contract files under ecs/, caller workflow using tanya-ok/ecs-contract. Config maps onto the contract without strain: BOARD_SIZE, RULESET, SUPERKO, KOMI, LOG_LEVEL, PORT as parameters; database password as a pointer; certificate bundle as a parameter; archive token from a vault. All three source kinds earn their place.

Repo smallest-board-infrastructure: cluster, service, roles, log group, the secret resource created without a value, the pointer parameters, and the service pointed at the live revision through the Stage 3 construct.

Name avoids the golang collision. Everything synthetic: no real account ids, ARNs, service or vault names. Minimum bar is a pair that synthesizes and passes the check; deploying against a real account is a stretch goal.
acceptance_criteria: Offline demo visibly reproduces and prevents a configuration reset, rejects a stale plan and invalid declaration, and never displays secret values.
notes:
Most useful after Stage 2 (resolver) and Stage 3 (live-revision construct), since the deploy half is what the demo shows.

Players are Alice and Bob, the canonical two parties from cryptographic protocol descriptions. Alice plays White, Bob plays Black. That follows Go convention rather than contradicting it: White is traditionally the senior seat, the teacher or stronger player, while Black takes the first move as compensation. Go has no gendered convention for colours.

The demo turns this into its point. Bob moves first and, under perfect play on 3x3, wins the whole board: the first move here is worth everything there is. The KOMI parameter is what balances a game, and on this board a fair komi would be 9, the entire board, which makes the compensation absurd. Alice, in the senior seat, can only choose how precisely to lose. A service whose configuration decides who can possibly win is a good demo for a contract about who owns which value.
Frontend (added 2026-09-27): a small browser UI served by the smallest-board service itself at /, so the demo stays two repos and one deployable. Plain HTML and JavaScript, no framework, no build step. A 3x3 board where the visitor plays Bob or Alice against the oracle, with the oracle's verdict for the current position. A footer shows the running task definition revision and the non-secret parameters (RULESET, SUPERKO, KOMI), so a deploy or a drift is visible on the page. Secret values never reach the page.
2026-10-07 coordinator: first increment is a local credential-free deterministic board showing conflicting writers, preserved setting, stale-plan denial and bad declaration. Full Go rules, oracle, database, new remote repositories, publication and live AWS remain later separately authorized work.

title: Distinguish secret read errors from confirmed missing keys
description: Portfolio review reproduced _has_json_key returning False for mocked ThrottlingException and DecryptionFailure while AccessDeniedException returns None. The caller reports False as a missing JSON key, conflating unreadable with absent. Model finding F1 in run 20261007T123322520415Z. Add cases for throttling, decryption failure, absent secret, invalid JSON and genuinely absent key. Choose an explicit unknown/error policy and actionable fixed diagnostics; do not automatically change deployment refusal into success just because the model suggested warn-and-bind. No live AWS calls were made.
close_reason: Implemented distinct probe states for confirmed missing key, missing secret, invalid JSON, access denial and read failure. Throttling, decryption and transport failures stop render with fixed safe diagnostics; explicit AccessDenied retains documented unverified-binding warning. 140 tests, lint, format and mypy passed using moto only. Local commit b94b9e9; no AWS deployment.
